evidence: src/infrastructure/OrderController.ts updateOrderState: `if (!state || !['paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered'].includes(state))` decides which target states are allowed, which is a domain state-transition rule.
src/infrastructure/OrderController.ts listOrdersByState: `['placed', 'paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered'].includes(state)` copies the domain's set of OrderState values by hand.
The two lists differ ('placed' is missing from the update list), which shows the controller enforces business policy, not just input format.
The rest of the file (req.body/params/query parsing, res.status(...).json(...), turning errors into a 400 response) is transport work that fits the infrastructure layer.
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
Most of OrderController is Express transport code, which belongs in infrastructure: it pulls values from the request and query, sends the work to the use cases, and turns results and errors into HTTP status codes and JSON. That part is fine.

`updateOrderState` goes further. It hardcodes the states an order may be moved to: ['paid', 'packed', 'shipped', 'delivered']. That list leaves out 'placed', even though the `listOrdersByState` list includes it. So this is not just a check that the value is a known OrderState. It encodes a rule from the domain state machine: an order can never be moved back to 'placed'. That rule belongs in the domain (the Order entity or the OrderState rules), or at least in the application use case, not in a transport adapter.

Both methods also copy the set of OrderState values by hand instead of taking it from the domain. This is smaller, but it is the same problem. The main misplaced responsibility is the transition-target rule.

violations.message: updateOrderState hardcodes the allowed target states ['paid','packed','shipped','delivered'] and leaves out 'placed'. This is a domain state-transition rule (domain layer) sitting in an infrastructure HTTP controller. It should live in the Order domain model or the UpdateOrderStateUseCase.
